claims.claim: The occupancy of substrate binding sites in wild-type DAT is inhibitory to the AIM-100 effects on DAT.
claims.source: These experiments provide additional evidence that the occupancy of substrate binding sites in wild-type DAT is inhibitory to the AIM-100 effects on DAT and suggest that the shift to an OC/IF conformation is not sufficient for AIM-100 induced oligomerization and endocytosis of the wild-type DAT when substrates or inhibitors are present.
claims.evidence: Inferred from substrate and inhibitor effects shown in Figures 5-6.

claims.claim: The shift to an OC/IF conformation is not sufficient for AIM-100 induced oligomerization and endocytosis of the wild-type DAT when substrates or inhibitors are present.
claims.source: These experiments provide additional evidence that the occupancy of substrate binding sites in wild-type DAT is inhibitory to the AIM-100 effects on DAT and suggest that the shift to an OC/IF conformation is not sufficient for AIM-100 induced oligomerization and endocytosis of the wild-type DAT when substrates or inhibitors are present.
claims.evidence: Inferred from modafinil effects which stabilize OC/IF states but still inhibit AIM-100 effects.

claims.claim: AIM-100 (20 µM) consistently and statistically significantly decreased the Bmax value (an average decrease of 26%) but did not significantly affect KD values of [3-H]CFT binding to DAT.
claims.source: In five independent experiments AIM-100 (20 µM) consistently and statistically significantly decreased the Bmax value (an average decrease of 26%) but did not significantly affect KD values (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: Measured in radioligand binding assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: The effect of AIM-100 on CFT binding parameters is consistent with the hypothesis that this effect involves an allosteric mechanism.
claims.source: Thus, the effect of AIM-100 on CFT binding parameters is consistent with the hypothesis that this effect involves an allosteric mechanism.
claims.evidence: Inferred from non-competitive binding pattern (decreased Bmax without affecting KD).

claims.claim: In AIM-100-treated cells YFP-HA-DAT was highly co-localized with Rab5 and EEA.1, markers of early and sorting endosomes.
claims.source: In AIM-100-treated cells YFP-HA-DAT was highly co-localized with Rab5 and EEA.1, markers of early and sorting endosomes, but not with Rab11 (Figure 7A), suggesting that DAT is not efficiently sorted to the recycling compartment.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by colocalization imaging in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: YFP-HA-DAT was not co-localized with Rab11 in AIM-100-treated cells, suggesting that DAT is not efficiently sorted to the recycling compartment.
claims.source: In AIM-100-treated cells YFP-HA-DAT was highly co-localized with Rab5 and EEA.1, markers of early and sorting endosomes, but not with Rab11 (Figure 7A), suggesting that DAT is not efficiently sorted to the recycling compartment.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by lack of colocalization with Rab11 in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Only a minimal amount of YFP-HA-DAT was detected in Rab7- and LysoTrackerRed-labeled compartments, indicating that DAT is not sorted to late endosomes and lysosomes after AIM-100-induced internalization.
claims.source: Only a minimal amount of YFP-HA-DAT was detected in Rab7- and LysoTrackerRed-labeled compartments, indicating that DAT is not sorted to late endosomes and lysosomes after AIM-100-induced internalization (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by minimal colocalization in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: AIM-100 did not induce degradation of YFP-HA-DAT or YFP-DAT in contrast to a substantial PKC-dependent degradation of the transporter in cells treated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA).
claims.source: AIM-100 did not induce degradation of YFP-HA-DAT or YFP-DAT in contrast to a substantial PKC-dependent degradation of the transporter in cells treated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) (Figure 8B–C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments in Figure 8B-C.

claims.claim: AIM-100 does not significantly increase YFP-HA-DAT ubiquitination.
claims.source: This result is consistent with the observation that AIM-100 does not significantly increase YFP-HA-DAT ubiquitination (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and ubiquitin blotting in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: YFP-HA-DAT labeled with HA11 and internalized in the presence of AIM-100 for 1.5 hr followed by 1.5 hr chase incubation without AIM-100 did not re-distribute from endosomes to the cell surface (recycling).
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, YFP-HA-DAT was labeled with HA11 and internalized in the presence of AIM-100 for 1.5 hr followed by washing and further incubating the cells at 37°C without AIM-100. This 1.5 hr chase incubation did not lead to re-distribution of YFP-HA-DAT from endosomes to the cell surface (recycling), but unexpectedly, actually resulted in an augmented accumulation of YFP-HA-DAT in endosomes (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by antibody uptake and chase experiments in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Cocaine did not prevent additional endocytosis of HA11:YFP-HA-DAT complexes during the chase incubation after AIM-100 treatment.
claims.source: Cocaine did not prevent additional endocytosis of HA11:YFP-HA-DAT complexes during the chase incubation (Figure 9), suggesting that cocaine binding must precede AIM-100 treatment in order for cocaine to inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by chase experiments with cocaine in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Cocaine binding must precede AIM-100 treatment in order for cocaine to inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
claims.source: Cocaine did not prevent additional endocytosis of HA11:YFP-HA-DAT complexes during the chase incubation (Figure 9), suggesting that cocaine binding must precede AIM-100 treatment in order for cocaine to inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from timing-dependent effects of cocaine shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: AIM-100 has effects on DAT that are not readily reversible.
claims.source: Importantly, these data indicate that AIM-100 has effects on DAT that are not readily reversible, and that DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 is not measurably recycled.
claims.evidence: Inferred from lack of recycling during chase incubation shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 is not measurably recycled.
claims.source: Importantly, these data indicate that AIM-100 has effects on DAT that are not readily reversible, and that DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 is not measurably recycled.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by lack of surface redistribution during chase in Figure 9.

claims.claim: AIM-100 did not inhibit recycling of DAT that had been internalized upon PKC activation and protected from AIM-100-induced endocytosis by cocaine.
claims.source: In contrast, AIM-100 did not inhibit recycling of DAT that had been internalized upon PKC activation and protected from AIM-100-induced endocytosis by cocaine (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by PMA/cocaine/AIM-100 experiments in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: AIM-100 does not affect the recycling process per se but acts in a cargo-specific fashion by blocking recycling of DAT exclusively only if DAT internalization is induced by AIM-100.
claims.source: These data suggest that AIM-100 does not affect the recycling process per se but acts in a cargo-specific fashion by blocking recycling of DAT exclusively only if DAT internalization is induced by AIM-100.
claims.evidence: Inferred from differential effects on PMA-induced versus AIM-100-induced internalized DAT.

claims.claim: The robust AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is at least partially due to an inability of DAT to recycle in the presence of AIM-100.
claims.source: The data in Figure 9 together with the observations of (i) linear kinetics of DAT accumulation in endosomes (Figure 1C); and (ii) lack of DAT in Rab11 recycling endosomes (Figure 7) suggest that the robust AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is at least partially due to an inability of DAT to recycle in the presence of AIM-100.
claims.evidence: Inferred from combination of recycling, kinetics, and localization data.

claims.claim: The extent of endosomal accumulation of DAT due to its constitutive internalization in the presence of monensin was significantly smaller than in the presence of AIM-100.
claims.source: However, the extent of endosomal accumulation of DAT due to its constitutive internalization in the presence of monensin was found to be significantly smaller than in the presence of AIM-100, and the monensin-dependent accumulation was not inhibited by cocaine (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by comparison experiments in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Monensin-dependent accumulation of DAT was not inhibited by cocaine.
claims.source: However, the extent of endosomal accumulation of DAT due to its constitutive internalization in the presence of monensin was found to be significantly smaller than in the presence of AIM-100, and the monensin-dependent accumulation was not inhibited by cocaine (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is the result of a combination of an ineffective recycling and an accelerated endocytosis, which is regulated by the mechanism apparently different from that of the constitutive endocytosis revealed in the presence of monensin.
claims.source: Therefore, AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is the result of a combination of an ineffective recycling and an accelerated endocytosis, which is regulated by the mechanism apparently different from that of the constitutive endocytosis revealed in the presence of monensin.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of AIM-100 and monensin effects.

claims.claim: siRNA knock-down of Ack1 (65–80% depletion) did not lead to YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis or other visible changes in the pattern of YFP-HA-DAT localization when compared with the control cells.
claims.source: siRNA knock-down of Ack1 (65–80% depletion, Figure 10A) did not lead to YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis or other visible changes in the pattern of YFP-HA-DAT localization when compared with the control cells (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by imaging of Ack1-depleted cells in Figure 10A-B.

claims.claim: AIM-100 caused robust YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis in Ack1-depleted cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, AIM-100 caused robust YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis in Ack1-depleted cells (Figure 10C) as evident by the strong increase in YFP-HA-DAT co-localization with Tfn-TxR in endosomes (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and colocalization analysis in Figure 10C-D.

claims.claim: KRCA-0008, a highly efficient inhibitor of Ack1 (IC50 = 18 nM), did not induce YFP-HA-DAT oligomerization and endocytosis at concentrations of 2–20 µM.
claims.source: Finally, another highly efficient inhibitor of Ack1 (KRCA-0008, IC50 = 18 nM) (Park et al., 2013) did not induce YFP-HA-DAT oligomerization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A) and endocytosis at concentrations of 2–20 µM (Figure 10F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and Western blot in Figure 10F and Figure 10—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: AIM-100 induced DAT endocytosis is Ack1-independent in PAE cells.
claims.source: Thus, together the data in Figure 10 indicate that AIM-100 induced DAT endocytosis is Ack1-independent in PAE cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from Ack1 knockdown and KRCA-0008 experiments in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Knock-down of clathrin heavy chain (CHC) had no inhibitory effect on AIM-100 induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis and oligomerization.
claims.source: Knock-down of clathrin heavy chain (CHC) had no inhibitory effect on AIM-100 induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis (Figure 10A–C) and oligomerization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B), whereas Tfn-TxR endocytosis was strongly inhibited as would be expected (Figure 10B, insets; and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by CHC knockdown experiments in Figure 10A-C and Figure 10—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Tfn-TxR endocytosis was strongly inhibited by CHC knockdown.
claims.source: Knock-down of clathrin heavy chain (CHC) had no inhibitory effect on AIM-100 induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis (Figure 10A–C) and oligomerization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B), whereas Tfn-TxR endocytosis was strongly inhibited as would be expected (Figure 10B, insets; and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10B insets and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: CHC knockdown caused a partial inhibition of the constitutive endocytosis of DAT observed in the presence of monensin.
claims.source: On the other hand, CHC knockdown caused a partial inhibition of the constitutive endocytosis of DAT observed in the presence of monensin (Figure 10—figure supplement 3) [also see (Sorkina et al., 2005)].
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: AIM-100 re-directs DAT to a specific endocytosis pathway rather than abolishing the plasma membrane retention of DAT.
claims.source: These data suggest that AIM-100 re-directs DAT to a specific endocytosis pathway rather than abolishing the plasma membrane retention of DAT.
claims.evidence: Inferred from differential effects of CHC knockdown on AIM-100-induced versus constitutive endocytosis.

claims.claim: AIM-100-induced endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT was not significantly inhibited by dynamin-2 siRNA knock-down.
claims.source: Surprisingly, AIM-100-induced endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT was not significantly inhibited by dynamin-2 siRNA knock-down (Figure 11A) and overexpression of the K44A dominant-negative dynamin mutant (data not shown).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by dynamin-2 knockdown experiments in Figure 11A.

claims.claim: Latranculin B (inhibitor of cortical actin cytoskeleton), ML141 (cdc42 inhibitor) and nystatin (cholesterol-chelating drug) did not affect AIM-100-dependent DAT endocytosis.
claims.source: Latranculin B (inhibitor of cortical actin cytoskeleton), ML141 (cdc42 inhibitor) and nystatin (cholesterol-chelating drug) also did not affect AIM-100-dependent DAT endocytosis (Figure 11B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibitor experiments in Figure 11B.

claims.claim: The PKC inhibitor, Go6976, did not block AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
claims.source: Further, the PKC inhibitor, Go6976, did not block AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 (likely referring to Figure 9—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: ML141 treatment induced a moderate endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT, suggesting that cdc42 could be involved in DAT retention at the cell surface.
claims.source: ML141 treatment induced a moderate endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT (Figure 11B), suggesting that cdc42 could be involved in DAT retention at the cell surface.
claims.evidence: Observed in Figure 11B and inferred from the effect of cdc42 inhibition.

claims.claim: An inhibitor of phospholipase D, FIPI reduced AIM-100-induced endocytosis two-fold.
claims.source: Interestingly, an inhibitor of phospholipase D, FIPI reduced AIM-100-induced endocytosis two-fold.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 11B.

claims.claim: The involvement of phospholipase D may be attributed to the importance of the product of phospholipase D activity, phosphatidic acid, in membrane fission and fusion processes.
claims.source: The involvement of phospholipase D may be attributed to the importance of the product of phospholipase D activity, phosphatidic acid, in membrane fission and fusion processes (Donaldson, 2009).
claims.evidence: Inferred from known functions of phosphatidic acid cited from literature.

claims.claim: Src kinase family inhibitor, PP2, and genistein, a wide-range tyrosine kinase inhibitor, did not alter the subcellular distribution of YFP-HA-DAT in untreated or AIM-100-treated PAE cells.
claims.source: Src kinase family inhibitor, PP2, and genistein, a wide-range tyrosine kinase inhibitor, did not alter the subcellular distribution of YFP-HA-DAT in untreated or AIM-100-treated PAE cells (data not shown).
claims.evidence: Stated as experimental observation without shown data.

claims.claim: AIM-100 induces DAT endocytosis via a novel CIE mechanism that does not involve caveolae-, CLIC/GEEC-, Arf6-, Rho-family-GTPase- and endophilin-dependent pathways, as well as micropinocytosis.
claims.source: These experiments ruled out the involvement of many known CIE mechanisms, such as those underlying caveolae-, CLIC/GEEC-, Arf6-, Rho-family-GTPase- and endophilin-dependent pathways, as well as micropinocytosis (Boucrot et al., 2015; Mayor et al., 2014). Thus, collectively the data in Figures 10 and 11 suggest that AIM-100 induces DAT endocytosis via a novel CIE mechanism.
claims.evidence: Inferred from negative results with multiple pathway inhibitors and cited literature on CIE mechanisms.

claims.claim: DAT is responsible for the clearance of dopamine released from synapses, and therefore, controls the duration and amplitude of dopamine signaling in the brain.
claims.source: DAT is responsible for the clearance of dopamine released from synapses, and therefore, controls the duration and amplitude of dopamine signaling in the brain (Giros et al., 1991; Jaber et al., 1997; Kristensen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from established literature on DAT function.

claims.claim: DAT is the principal target of psychostimulants like cocaine and amphetamines.
claims.source: DAT is also known to be the principal target of psychostimulants like cocaine and amphetamines (Gainetdinov and Caron, 2003; Gowrishankar et al., 2014; Spiga et al., 2008; Volkow and Morales, 2015; Willuhn et al., 2010; Wise, 2008).
claims.evidence: Cited from established literature on psychostimulant pharmacology.

claims.claim: DAT belongs to the high-affinity saline carrier (SLC) six gene family of Na+, Cl--dependent transporters consisting of 12 TM domains, and cytosolic N- and C-terminal tails.
claims.source: DAT belongs to the high-affinity saline carrier (SLC) six gene family of Na+, Cl--dependent transporters consisting of 12 TM domains, and cytosolic N- and C-terminal tails (Kristensen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from established structural knowledge of DAT.

claims.claim: DAT is proposed to form dimers and high-order oligomers, although the mechanisms of oligomerization are not understood.
claims.source: DAT is proposed to form dimers and high-order oligomers, although the mechanisms of oligomerization are not understood (Hastrup et al., 2001; Hastrup et al., 2003; Li et al., 2010; Sorkina et al., 2003; Torres et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies on DAT oligomerization.

claims.claim: DAT dimerization/multimerization modulates the substrate transport activity of DAT and is necessary for the effective transport of newly-synthesized DAT from the endoplasmic reticulum.
claims.source: It has been proposed that DAT dimerization/multimerization modulates the substrate transport activity of DAT and is necessary for the effective transport of newly-synthesized DAT from the endoplasmic reticulum (Chen and Reith, 2008; Sorkina et al., 2003; Torres et al., 2003; Zhen et al., 2015; Zhen and Reith, 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous functional studies of DAT oligomerization.

claims.claim: DAT has been shown to internalize in response to protein kinase C (PKC) activation, amphetamines, substrates, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, neuronal activity and inhibition of Ack1.
claims.source: DAT has been shown to internalize in response to protein kinase C (PKC) activation, amphetamines, substrates, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, neuronal activity and inhibition of Ack1 (Activated Cdc42 Kinase) (Eriksen et al., 2009; Gabriel et al., 2013; Hoover et al., 2007; Huff et al., 1997; Melikian and Buckley, 1999; Rao et al., 2012; Richardson et al., 2016; Sorkina et al., 2003; Vaughan et al., 1997; Wheeler et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies on DAT endocytosis regulation.

claims.claim: DAT appears to be capable of internalization through both CME and CIE.
claims.source: DAT appears to be capable of internalization through both CME and CIE (Cremona et al., 2011; Gabriel et al., 2013; Sorkina et al., 2013; Sorkina et al., 2005; Wheeler et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies on DAT endocytosis mechanisms.

claims.claim: The strong effect of AIM-100 on DAT oligomerization is the first example of a chemically-enhanced non-covalent oligomerization of a multi-spanning TM protein.
claims.source: To our knowledge, the strong effect of AIM-100 on DAT oligomerization is the first example of a chemically-enhanced non-covalent oligomerization of a multi-spanning TM protein.
claims.evidence: Stated as a novel finding based on authors' knowledge of the field.

claims.claim: The bacterial homolog of DAT LeuT was crystalized as a dimer.
claims.source: Whereas the bacterial homolog of DAT LeuT was crystalized as a dimer (Yamashita et al., 2005), Drosophila DAT was crystallized as a monomer (Penmatsa et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from structural biology literature.

claims.claim: Drosophila DAT was crystallized as a monomer.
claims.source: Whereas the bacterial homolog of DAT LeuT was crystalized as a dimer (Yamashita et al., 2005), Drosophila DAT was crystallized as a monomer (Penmatsa et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from structural biology literature.

claims.claim: The 'minimal' DAT oligomer detected at ~290 kDa for YFP-HA-DAT and ~190 kDa for HA-DAT may correspond to a trimer.
claims.source: Detection of a 290 kDa species of YFP-DAT/YFP-HA-DAT (Figures 1, 4, 5, 6 and 8 and supplements) and a 190 kDa species of HA-DAT (Figure 2D) suggests that this 'minimal' DAT oligomer may correspond to a trimer.
claims.evidence: Inferred from molecular weight calculations based on Western blot data.

claims.claim: Chemical cross-linking of Cys246 and Cys306 results in the formation of dimers, trimers and tetramers of DAT.
claims.source: Although DAT and other SLC6 transporters are typically thought to be dimers, it was reported that chemical cross-linking of Cys246 and Cys306 results in the formation of dimers, trimers and tetramers of DAT (Hastrup et al., 2001; Hastrup et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous cross-linking studies.

claims.claim: Despite the structural similarity of catecholamine transporters, their oligomerization mechanisms might be fundamentally different.
claims.source: The fact that similar SDS-resistant oligomeric species of NET and SERT were not detected in the absence or presence of AIM-100 implies that despite the structural similarity of catecholamine transporters and contrary to a generally accepted notion of an equivalence in their oligomerization mechanisms (Alguel et al., 2016), these mechanisms might actually be fundamentally different.
claims.evidence: Inferred from differential oligomerization responses to AIM-100 among DAT, NET, and SERT.

claims.claim: An interaction of SERT with phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is important for the formation of stable oligomers of SERT.
claims.source: For example, an interaction of SERT with phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) was recently demonstrated to be important for the formation of stable oligomers of SERT (Anderluh et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from recent SERT oligomerization study.

claims.claim: The PIP2-dependent oligomerization mechanism may not be involved in DAT oligomerization.
claims.source: However, this mechanism may not be involved in DAT oligomerization. DAT has been shown to be oligomeric in endosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum (Sorkina et al., 2003; Zhen and Reith, 2018), where PIP2 is present at extremely low levels (Hammond and Balla, 2015).
claims.evidence: Inferred from DAT oligomerization in compartments lacking PIP2.

claims.claim: Differences in the sites of PIP2 binding to DAT and SERT (amino-terminus versus transmembrane core, respectively) may be responsible for different mechanisms of their oligomerization.
claims.source: It is possible that differences in the sites of PIP2 binding to DAT and SERT (amino-terminus versus transmembrane core, respectively) (Buchmayer et al., 2013; Hamilton et al., 2014) are responsible for different mechanisms of their oligomerization.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on cited differences in PIP2 binding sites.

claims.claim: Formation of highly stable oligomers and DAT clustering in living cells correlated with DAT endocytosis in experiments that examined the effects of transporter inhibitors and substrates, and compared AIM-100 effects on three monoamine transporters.
claims.source: Formation of highly stable oligomers and DAT clustering in living cells correlated with DAT endocytosis in experiments that examined the effects of transporter inhibitors and substrates, and compared AIM-100 effects on three monoamine transporters (Figures 4–6).
claims.evidence: Observed correlation across multiple experimental conditions in Figures 4-6.

claims.claim: The fast kinetics of AIM-100-induced clustering of DAT suggests that DAT oligomerization and clustering are part of the mechanism mediating AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
claims.source: These observations together with the fast kinetics of AIM-100-induced clustering of DAT (Figure 3B–C) suggest that DAT oligomerization and clustering are part of the mechanism mediating AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from temporal relationship between clustering and endocytosis.

claims.claim: The dramatic accumulation of DAT in endosomes following AIM-100 treatment is a synergistic effect due to both accelerated endocytosis and inefficient recycling.
claims.source: Several lines of evidence suggest that such a dramatic accumulation is a synergistic effect due to both accelerated endocytosis and inefficient recycling (Figures 7–9).
claims.evidence: Inferred from combined data on endocytosis kinetics, localization, and recycling experiments.

claims.claim: In early endosomes DAT oligomers are not efficiently packaged into tubular recycling carriers due to the large size of these oligomers.
claims.source: We propose that in early endosomes DAT oligomers are not efficiently packaged into tubular recycling carriers due to the large size of these oligomers.
claims.evidence: Proposed mechanism based on oligomer size and recycling data.

claims.claim: When monomeric receptors that normally recycle are crosslinked by multivalent ligands, these receptors are partially mis-targeted to the lysosomal pathway.
claims.source: When monomeric receptors that normally recycle are crosslinked by multivalent ligands, these receptors have been shown to be partially mis-targeted to the lysosomal pathway (Geuze et al., 1987; Hopkins and Trowbridge, 1983).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies on receptor trafficking.

claims.claim: Targeting of non-ubiquitinated cargo to lysosomes may occur on a substantially longer time scale than 2 hr.
claims.source: It is possible that targeting of non-ubiquitinated cargo to lysosomes occurs on a substantially longer time scale than our 2 hr time-course experiments (Tewari et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Speculated based on cited literature on lysosomal targeting kinetics.

claims.claim: The pathways and mechanisms of DAT endocytosis in the presence of AIM-100 observed by Wu and co-workers and in the present study may be different.
claims.source: This raises a question of whether the pathways and mechanisms of DAT endocytosis in the presence of AIM-100 observed by Wu and co-workers (Wu et al., 2015) and in the present study are different.
claims.evidence: Questioned based on differences in clathrin and cdc42 dependence between studies.

claims.claim: Considerable general toxicity of pitstop-2 has been reported.
claims.source: However, considerable general toxicity of this compound has been reported (Lemmon and Traub, 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Willox et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from literature on pitstop-2 toxicity.

claims.claim: Pitstop-2 has been shown to strongly block CIE.
claims.source: Pitstop-2 has also been shown to strongly block the CIE (Dutta et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from literature on pitstop-2 effects.

claims.claim: Although Ack1 was reported to be associated with the clathrin coated structures, the importance of Ack1 for CME has not been established.
claims.source: Furthermore, although Ack1 was reported to be associated with the clathrin coated structures, the importance of Ack1 for CME has not been established (Shen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Cited from literature on Ack1 localization and function.

claims.claim: Screening for kinases involved in DAT regulation did not reveal the involvement of Ack1.
claims.source: Finally, it should be noted that screening for kinases involved in DAT regulation did not reveal the involvement of Ack1 (Vuorenpää et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: Cited from kinase screening study.

claims.claim: AIM-100 increases DAT oligomerization by directly interacting with DAT in its conformation favorable for oligomerization and thus stabilizing DAT trimers/oligomers.
claims.source: First, we propose that AIM-100 increases DAT oligomerization by directly interacting with DAT in its conformation favorable for oligomerization and thus stabilizing DAT trimers/oligomers.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings.

claims.claim: The AIM-100:DAT interaction and the occupancy of the substrate binding sites are mutually exclusive.
claims.source: We also suggest that the AIM-100:DAT interaction and the occupancy of the substrate binding sites are mutually exclusive.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on inhibitor/substrate competition data.

claims.claim: DAT oligomerization results in extensive surface clustering, which may be driven by the hydrophobic mismatch of oligomers and the membrane.
claims.source: Second, we propose that DAT oligomerization results in an extensive surface clustering, which may be driven by the hydrophobic mismatch of oligomers and the membrane.
claims.evidence: Proposed mechanism based on biophysical principles.

claims.claim: Clustering is typically observed as the consequence of ligand-induced dimerization of receptors.
claims.source: Clustering is typically observed as the consequence of ligand-induced dimerization of receptors [for example (Zidovetzki et al., 1981; Zidovetzki et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: Cited from literature on receptor clustering.

claims.claim: DAT clusters may stabilize or promote spontaneous membrane invagination and scission leading to a coat-independent endocytosis.
claims.source: Third, DAT clusters may stabilize or promote spontaneous membrane invagination and scission leading to a coat-independent endocytosis.
claims.evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: TM cargo-induced membrane remodeling has been proposed.
claims.source: Such TM cargo-induced membrane remodeling has been proposed (Johannes and Mayor, 2010; Johannes et al., 2014), although experimentally-proven examples in intact cells or in vitro are rare (Callenberg et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2012; Rosholm et al., 2017; Spoden et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Cited from literature on cargo-induced membrane remodeling.

claims.claim: Independence of the AIM-100-induced endocytosis of clathrin, dynamin and other mechanisms mediating various known CIE pathways supports the hypothesis that this endocytosis may not involve a specific membrane bending/scission machinery.
claims.source: Independence of the AIM-100-induced endocytosis of clathrin, dynamin and other mechanisms mediating various known CIE pathways, supports the hypothesis that this endocytosis may not involve a specific membrane bending/scission machinery.
claims.evidence: Inferred from negative results with multiple pathway inhibitors.

claims.claim: Coat-free endocytosis may serve as part of the regulatory and quality-control mechanisms that remove excess DAT from the cell surface in the absence of extracellular substrates and may clear DAT oligomers as they are functionally impaired.
claims.source: Our findings inevitably lead to a hypothesis that coat-free endocytosis may serve as part of the regulatory and quality-control mechanisms that remove excess DAT from the cell surface in the absence of extracellular substrates and may clear DAT oligomers as they are functionally impaired (Zhen and Reith, 2018).
claims.evidence: Hypothesized based on findings and cited literature on DAT oligomer function.

results.result: AIM-100 induces dramatic oligomerization and endocytosis of DAT in multiple cell types and primary neurons. Treatment with AIM-100 (≥10 µM) causes redistribution of DAT from the plasma membrane to intracellular vesicles with linear kinetics over 2 hours, resulting in ~75% reduction in surface DAT and >5-fold increase in SDS-resistant oligomers (~290 kDa). Oligomers are enriched in endosomes compared to the plasma membrane and are not formed through disulfide bonds.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C32 are strongly supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches including live-cell imaging (C12-C13), quantitative antibody uptake assays (C14-C16), Western blotting with biotinylation (C16-C27), and validation in multiple cell lines and primary neurons (C28-C32). The linear kinetics (R²=0.9693, C14), dose-response relationship (C13), and biochemical quantification (C16-C17, C22-C23) provide robust evidence. The resistance to reducing agents (C20-C21) appropriately rules out disulfide-mediated oligomerization.

results.result: AIM-100 induces rapid clustering of DAT on the cell surface that precedes endocytosis. TIR-FM imaging reveals dramatic increase in diffraction-limited DAT spots (<200 nm) that peak at 10-20 minutes and gradually decline over 30 minutes. Approximately 35% of spots persist for >1 hour while others are transient (few minutes), with some spots showing lateral movement characteristic of endocytic vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are well-supported by TIR-FM time-lapse imaging data (Figure 3A-D). The temporal relationship between clustering (peaking at 10-20 min, C34) and endocytosis kinetics (linear over 2 hr, C14) supports the inference that clustering precedes endocytosis (C39). The quantitative analysis of spot dynamics (C35) and visual observations of lateral movement (C36) provide direct evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: FRET measurements demonstrate increased DAT oligomerization in living cells treated with AIM-100. The intensity of FRET from CFP to YFP was significantly higher in plasma membrane clusters and intracellular vesicles of AIM-100-treated cells compared to vehicle-treated cells, indicating higher probability or increased stability of DAT-DAT interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by sensitized FRET measurements in cells co-expressing CFP-DAT and YFP-DAT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). The significant increase in FRETN values in AIM-100-treated cells provides direct evidence of enhanced oligomerization in living cells. The interpretation (C41) appropriately reflects established FRET principles linking increased FRET efficiency to closer proximity and/or increased stability of protein-protein interactions.

results.result: AIM-100 effects are specific to DAT and do not induce oligomerization or endocytosis of the closely related transporters NET and SERT. Live-cell imaging and Western blotting show that GFP-NET and GFP-SERT remain predominantly monomeric and do not undergo clustering or endocytosis in response to AIM-100, demonstrating correlation between oligomerization and endocytosis specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C42-C44 are well-supported by parallel experiments with NET and SERT (Figure 4). The negative results with structurally similar transporters strengthen the specificity argument and support the correlation between oligomerization and endocytosis (C44). The use of the same experimental conditions and detection methods (live-cell imaging and Western blotting) provides appropriate controls for the DAT experiments.

results.result: Cocaine inhibits AIM-100-induced DAT oligomerization and endocytosis in wild-type DAT but not in the W63A mutant, suggesting mutual exclusivity between AIM-100 effects and substrate binding site occupancy. The W63A mutation, which disrupts the outward-facing conformation and blocks cocaine binding, does not prevent AIM-100 effects, indicating that AIM-100 action does not require accessible substrate binding sites but cocaine binding can counteract AIM-100 effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C45-C51 are supported by experiments with cocaine and the W63A mutant (Figures 5A-H). The differential cocaine sensitivity between wild-type and W63A mutant provides strong evidence for the mutual exclusivity hypothesis (C3) and suggests an allosteric mechanism. However, the inference that AIM-100 binds to DAT (C4) remains indirect; while consistent with the data, direct binding evidence is not provided. The cited literature on W63A properties (C47-C48) appropriately supports the interpretation.

results.result: DAT substrates (dopamine, amphetamine) and the atypical inhibitor modafinil significantly reduce AIM-100-induced DAT oligomerization and endocytosis. These results demonstrate that occupancy of substrate binding sites inhibits AIM-100 effects and suggest that conformational shifts to occluded/inward-facing states are insufficient for AIM-100 action when substrates or inhibitors are bound.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by experiments with substrates and modafinil (Figure 6). The consistent inhibitory effects across multiple ligands strengthen the conclusion about substrate binding site occupancy (C54). The interpretation regarding conformational states (C55) is reasonable given the cited literature on modafinil's effects, though the conformational state inference is indirect. The data support mutual exclusivity between ligand binding and AIM-100 effects.

results.result: AIM-100 decreases the Bmax of [³H]CFT binding to DAT by 26% without significantly affecting KD values, consistent with a non-competitive, allosteric mechanism of action. This binding pattern was observed consistently across five independent experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by radioligand binding assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B). The statistical significance of Bmax decrease with unchanged KD across five experiments provides robust evidence for non-competitive inhibition. The interpretation of an allosteric mechanism (C57) is appropriate for this binding pattern. However, the experiments were performed at 20°C rather than 37°C to minimize endocytosis, which may affect the quantitative parameters.

results.result: Internalized DAT accumulates in early/sorting endosomes (Rab5+, EEA.1+) but not in recycling endosomes (Rab11-), late endosomes (Rab7-), or lysosomes (LysoTracker-) following AIM-100 treatment. AIM-100 does not induce DAT degradation or ubiquitination, contrasting with PMA-induced PKC-dependent degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are well-supported by colocalization studies with endosomal markers (Figures 7-8) and cycloheximide chase experiments (Figure 8B-C). The high colocalization with early endosome markers (C58) and minimal colocalization with late endosome/lysosome markers (C60) are clearly demonstrated. The lack of degradation (C61) and ubiquitination (C62) over 2 hours is appropriately documented, though longer time courses might reveal eventual degradation.

results.result: DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 does not recycle back to the plasma membrane during chase incubation, and cocaine cannot prevent continued endocytosis during the chase period. In contrast, AIM-100 does not inhibit recycling of DAT internalized via PKC activation, indicating cargo-specific effects. The robust endosomal accumulation results from both accelerated endocytosis and blocked recycling.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70 are supported by antibody uptake and chase experiments (Figure 9 and supplements). The lack of recycling (C63, C67) and continued endocytosis during chase (C64) are clearly demonstrated. The differential effect on PMA-induced versus AIM-100-induced internalized DAT (C68-C69) provides strong evidence for cargo-specificity. The synthesis of multiple observations (C70) is well-reasoned, though the relative contributions of blocked recycling versus accelerated endocytosis are not quantitatively determined.

results.result: Monensin-induced constitutive DAT endocytosis results in significantly less endosomal accumulation than AIM-100-induced endocytosis, and monensin-dependent accumulation is not inhibited by cocaine. This indicates that AIM-100-induced accumulation involves both ineffective recycling and accelerated endocytosis via a mechanism distinct from constitutive endocytosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by comparison experiments with monensin (Figure 9—figure supplement 2). The quantitative difference in accumulation (C71) and differential cocaine sensitivity (C72) provide evidence for mechanistic differences. The conclusion (C73) appropriately synthesizes these observations, though the precise mechanisms underlying constitutive versus AIM-100-induced endocytosis remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis is independent of Ack1 in PAE cells. Ack1 knockdown (65-80% depletion) does not prevent AIM-100-induced endocytosis, and the specific Ack1 inhibitor KRCA-0008 (IC50=18 nM) does not induce DAT oligomerization or endocytosis at concentrations up to 20 µM.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are well-supported by Ack1 knockdown experiments and pharmacological inhibition (Figure 10A-F). The robust AIM-100-induced endocytosis in Ack1-depleted cells (C75) and lack of effect with KRCA-0008 (C76) provide strong evidence against Ack1 involvement. This contradicts previous reports and is appropriately acknowledged in the Discussion. The cell-type specificity caveat is noted but does not undermine the conclusion for PAE cells.

results.result: Clathrin heavy chain (CHC) knockdown does not inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis or oligomerization, while strongly inhibiting transferrin endocytosis as expected. However, CHC knockdown partially inhibits constitutive DAT endocytosis induced by monensin, suggesting that AIM-100 redirects DAT to a clathrin-independent pathway rather than simply disrupting membrane retention.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by CHC knockdown experiments (Figure 10A-C and supplements). The differential effects on AIM-100-induced versus transferrin endocytosis (C78-C79) and constitutive DAT endocytosis (C80) provide strong evidence for pathway specificity. The interpretation that AIM-100 redirects rather than disrupts (C81) is well-reasoned based on the differential CHC dependence.

results.result: AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis occurs via a novel clathrin-independent mechanism that is independent of dynamin, cholesterol-rich microdomains, actin cytoskeleton, PKC, and multiple known CIE pathways (caveolae, CLIC/GEEC, Arf6, Rho-family GTPases, endophilin, micropinocytosis). Phospholipase D inhibition (FIPI) reduces endocytosis two-fold, and cdc42 inhibition (ML141) induces moderate DAT endocytosis, suggesting cdc42 involvement in surface retention.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C82-C89 are supported by extensive pharmacological and genetic inhibition experiments (Figure 11). The negative results with multiple pathway inhibitors (C82-C84, C88) systematically rule out known mechanisms. The partial effect of FIPI (C86) suggests phospholipase D involvement, consistent with its role in membrane dynamics (C87). The ML141 effect (C85) is appropriately interpreted as affecting retention rather than AIM-100-induced endocytosis. The conclusion of a novel mechanism (C89) is well-justified by the comprehensive exclusion of known pathways.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanistic model where AIM-100 binds to DAT in a conformation favorable for oligomerization through an allosteric mechanism, leading to extensive surface clustering driven by hydrophobic mismatch. The clusters then undergo coat-independent endocytosis via spontaneous membrane invagination and scission, followed by endosomal retention. This may represent a quality-control mechanism for removing excess or oligomeric DAT from the cell surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C10-C11, C117-C119, C121, C123-C124 represent a proposed mechanistic model that integrates the experimental findings but includes substantial speculation. While the allosteric mechanism is supported by binding data (C10, C57), the direct binding of AIM-100 to DAT is not demonstrated (C117-C118). The clustering-driven endocytosis model (C119, C121) is plausible given the temporal relationships and independence from known machinery (C123), but direct evidence for cargo-induced membrane remodeling is lacking. The quality-control hypothesis (C124) is speculative. The model is internally consistent with the data but requires further validation.

results.result: Background claims about DAT function, structure, and regulation. DAT is responsible for dopamine clearance and is the principal target of psychostimulants. It belongs to the SLC6 family with 12 transmembrane domains and forms dimers/oligomers through unknown mechanisms. DAT oligomerization modulates transport activity and ER export, and DAT internalizes in response to multiple stimuli via both CME and CIE.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C96 are appropriately cited from established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. These background claims provide necessary context for the experimental work and are not contested by the current findings.

results.result: Discussion of DAT oligomerization in structural and mechanistic context. The authors claim this is the first example of chemically-enhanced non-covalent oligomerization of a multi-spanning transmembrane protein and discuss differences in oligomerization mechanisms between DAT, NET, and SERT, including potential roles of PIP2 binding site differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 involve interpretation and speculation about oligomerization mechanisms. The novelty claim (C97) may be overstated without comprehensive literature review. The molecular weight calculations suggesting trimers (C100) are reasonable but indirect. The proposed mechanistic differences between transporters (C102, C104-C105) are speculative, though consistent with the differential AIM-100 responses. The discussion appropriately acknowledges uncertainty but makes claims beyond what the data directly support.

results.result: Synthesis and interpretation of trafficking data. The authors argue that oligomerization and clustering correlate with and mechanistically drive endocytosis, and that dramatic endosomal accumulation results from synergistic effects of accelerated endocytosis and inefficient recycling. They propose that large oligomers cannot be efficiently packaged into recycling carriers and discuss potential lysosomal targeting on longer timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are well-supported by the correlation across multiple experimental conditions and temporal relationships. The proposed mechanism for recycling block (C109) is reasonable speculation based on oligomer size, though not directly tested. The comparison to receptor crosslinking (C110) and discussion of lysosomal targeting timescales (C111) appropriately contextualize the findings with cited literature.

results.result: Discussion of discrepancies with prior work and limitations of previous studies. The authors question whether their findings differ from Wu et al. (2015) regarding clathrin and cdc42 dependence, and discuss limitations of pitstop-2 as a clathrin inhibitor and uncertainties about Ack1's role in CME.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 appropriately acknowledge discrepancies with prior work and cite literature on methodological limitations (pitstop-2 toxicity, C113-C114). The discussion is balanced and identifies potential sources of differences between studies (cell types, methods) without dismissing prior work. This represents appropriate scientific discourse about conflicting findings.

results.result: Background on receptor clustering and cargo-induced membrane remodeling from literature. Clustering typically results from ligand-induced receptor dimerization, and transmembrane cargo-induced membrane remodeling has been proposed but rarely demonstrated experimentally.
results.evaluation: Claims C120 and C122 are appropriately cited from literature and provide context for the proposed mechanisms. These represent established concepts used to frame the current findings.
